Nvidia board reportedly meeting to oust Jensen Huang
The Nvidia board is reportedly preparing for an extraordinary meeting.
Several media are reporting that the board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after he allegedly had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.
The board is preparing to meet as soon as today, according to the Financial Times, to determine his future, people familiar with the matter said.
The stock is down over 7% in after-hours trade on the NASDAQ.
Cotton On pays penalties for alleged product safety reporting breaches

Clothing and retail company Cotton On has paid $19,800 in penalties after the consumer watchdog issued it two infringement notices for failing to comply with mandatory product safety reporting requirements on two occasions.
Cotton On allegedly failed to submit mandatory reports within the required two days after it became aware of serious injuries relating to two products supplied by its subsidiaries Supre and Typo.
The ACCC alleges the company failed to submit reports within the required time period for a Supre-branded pair of jeans and a Typo-branded Christmas snow globe.

"Mandatory reporting helps the ACCC identify potentially unsafe products quickly and act promptly to protect consumers from harm," ACCC commissioner Luke Woodward says."Suppliers must have systems in place to identify reportable incidents and notify the ACCC within the required two-day timeframe."
"Mandatory reporting helps the ACCC identify potentially unsafe products quickly and act promptly to protect consumers from harm," ACCC commissioner Luke Woodward says.
"Suppliers must have systems in place to identify reportable incidents and notify the ACCC within the required two-day timeframe."

The ACCC says Cotton On has undertaken a risk assessment and additional safety testing of both products, which confirmed the reported injuries did not arise from a defect or safety issue with the products.

"While the ACCC has not identified any safety concerns about the products, Cotton On's alleged reporting failures delayed important product-safety information reaching us," Mr Woodward says."The failure to report serious safety incidents quickly is serious because it may delay urgent safety action, including recalls, and could put other consumers at risk of injury or death."
"While the ACCC has not identified any safety concerns about the products, Cotton On's alleged reporting failures delayed important product-safety information reaching us," Mr Woodward says.
"The failure to report serious safety incidents quickly is serious because it may delay urgent safety action, including recalls, and could put other consumers at risk of injury or death."

The ACCC says Cotton On has committed to conducting regular audits of consumer complaints it receives where an injury or illness is recorded for three years, to assess whether it has complied with its mandatory reporting obligations.
ANZ boss says we're in a 'dangerous situation' with global markets
ANZ's chief executive Nuno Matos is asked about inflation in Australia and the link with capital investment and the AI and data centre build out.
Specifically, he's asked if the expenditure "supercycle", government expenditure, baked-in higher inflation, and rising interest rates, are a problem.
Mr Matos says the world is in a "dangerous situation" at the moment.
"Globally, undoubtedly, the combination of those four factors, and Australia is not different in that regard," he said.

"They are contributing to a competition for capital. We never saw this amount of spending in our lives, in our lifetimes. It's just if you add all of that mass of capital that is being required to fund all of these topics, as I said, AI, defence, infrastructure, government deficits in the past.

"So we have a very curious situation in the world where we have the equity markets at record highs, basically because of the tech wave and basically because of the AI wave, but at the same time you have record highs of interest rates.
"It's a dangerous situation for the world."
ANZ boss says AI has a 'dark side' and needs guardrails and global regulation
Matos says it's a very difficult technology to talk about in terms of the future, because whatever he says now could prove to be wrong in six months, because that's how quickly things are moving.
He then talks about the ways in which ANZ is dealing with AI and adapting to it. He says ANZ is building an AI academy to train its staff in how to use it.
But he says there are negative things about AI that we can't ignore:

"AI has a dark side," he says."AI can be used maliciously to [commit] fraud, to defraud customers, to scam customers, to impact critical infrastructure, being bank infrastructure, public infrastructure. That's very obvious."Which means that going into a wide adoption of AI without having the adequate guardrails, it's a big problem."
"AI has a dark side," he says.
"AI can be used maliciously to [commit] fraud, to defraud customers, to scam customers, to impact critical infrastructure, being bank infrastructure, public infrastructure. That's very obvious.
"Which means that going into a wide adoption of AI without having the adequate guardrails, it's a big problem."
He then talked about the impact of AI on employment, and the need for global regulation of the technology:
"On the job side, I can't tell you if AI will have a net positive, net negative, or neutral impact on jobs in the world or in Australia," he said.
"I can't tell you because if I tell you, I will be speculating. Everything is possible.
"I can only bring the following rationale. In the past, all technologies that were found in the world actually supported more employment and more growth. Until today, that has been the trend.

"The question is if AI will be different, meaning if some of those things we listen to, that AI will kill 50 per cent of jobs happens, [then we] will have a crisis and it's not going to be in Australia [only], it's going to be a global crisis.
"This is one of the few examples where I would say some global regulation is needed to make sure that society does not [get] into trouble."

ANZ boss says housing affordability is a global problem
Simon Kennedy, Liberal MP, asks ANZ's chief executive Nuno Matos if government spending is contributing to inflation.
Matos has no problem answering it (if he was a central banker he would say it's not his place to talk about this topic).
He says lower government spending would lead to lower inflation. He says it's "simple economics".
Kennedy then shifts to housing.
He says since property prices have fallen by 8%, has housing become more affordable?

He's citing some numbers from the Housing Industry Association, which has said that even though property prices have fallen this year, housing affordability remains 5.4 per cent worse than a year ago in Australia.

Matos says since house prices have fallen and people's incomes haven't fallen, by that equation housing would look more affordable on paper, but unfortunately interest payments have also gone up and people therefore aren't able to borrow as much for a home loan.
Matos makes the point that countries everywhere are dealing with housing affordability crises at the moment.
He says in his home country of Portugal, it's practically impossible for young people aspiring to home ownership to buy a home in the capital city.
The reality of offshoring
The conversation moves to ANZ's decision to offshore jobs.
ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos says offshoring has been practised for decades, and in fact, in 2026, the number of ANZ's offshore staff reduced by 600.
But he also says that some countries have evolved to specialise in some functions, which mean they can perform those functions better than Australian banks can do in Australia.
Committee chair Ed Husic notes that the average wage of ANZ's back office staff in India is $31,000 a year, and $62,000 for operations and tech staff.

He wonders if offshoring is more about reducing wages costs than anything else. He wonders if the bank is doing anything to increase the relevant skills of local workers so that it doesn't feel the need to offshore.
Nuno Matos says his banking group operates in 29 countries: in the United States, UK, Germany, the Middle East, and in most countries in Asia.

'Inexpensive tech stocks' drive Wall St gains, according to one analyst
Wall Street has closed for the day, with all three major markets closing in the green.
The S&P 500 finished up +1.3% to 7,619 points.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average has finished up +0.5% to 52,486 points.
The Nasdaq Composite has finished up +1.6% to 25,466 points.
Senior financial market analyst at capital.com, Kyle Rodda, says the gains were driven by investors picking up "inexpensive tech stocks".

"The ripple effect of the hotter than expected US CPI from a day earlier was still evident in price action. Traders continue to price in another rate hike from the Fed, with a slim but uncomfortable chance the central bank lifts by 50 basis points next month," he says.

"Cyclicals lagged the pack as a result. Meanwhile, rate-sensitive assets like precious metals pulled back in a session without price signals from the Treasury market because of its closure for the Veterans Day holiday.

"But the rebound in tech was more than enough to drive Wall Street higher as CoreWeave's results boosted confidence in the AI trade and earnings, a dearth of event risk following a heavy three weeks of news flow eased volatility, and historically cheap valuations attracted investors back into the market."
Mr Rodda says there have been four major drivers of volatility recently.

"The AI trade has been legged by disappointing quarterly results. New regulatory risk to AI in the US following midterm elections and a generally new hue to the American political complexion has hurt sentiment," he says.

"Interest rate uncertainty remains rife amid signs of stubborn price pressures around the globe. Geopolitical risk and energy market volatility have eased but still persist with little apparent progress in US-Iran peace talks.

"Barring a big, new surprise, this combination of factors will likely remain the main driver of global markets to end 2026, with market participants searching for earnings resilience, visibility about the peak in global rates, and an improvement in the US domestic and foreign political situation."
ANZ boss defends the profits his bank makes from mortgages
Committee chair, Labor MP Ed Husic, asks his first question about ANZ's profit. He said ANZ's recent full-year cash profit was $7.59 billion.
"How much is that up from last year?" he asked.
ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos replies:
"It's up 31% on a reported basis. On a real basis it's up 10%."
Husic says everyone in Australia seems to be going through tough times, except for Australia's largest businesses.

He says banks are making close to $300,000 profit from the average owner-occupier 30-year home loan of around $731,000. He says that profit is up $40,000 since interest rates started rising earlier this year.
He wonders how much profit ANZ is making a week from the typical home loan.
Matos says "the mortgage business is one of the least profitable businesses in banking in Australia, and it has reduced profitability year after year, at least in the last 20 years".
Matos says he would dispute the figures Husic has just cited, but says he also hasn't read the report from which those figures come.
He defends the operation of Australia's big banks and says they're "performing their role in delivering to society".
Committee chair lays out priorities
In his opening statement, House Economics Committee chair Ed Husic doesn't use hints ... he makes it pretty clear what he's keen to examine with the Big Four bank CEOs over the next two days.
"As evidenced by their recent results, Australia's major banks remain highly profitable," he said.
"There’s nothing inherently wrong with a profitable banking system.
"Australia needs strong, well-capitalised banks that can lend through difficult economic periods, investing in measures that keep people's money safe.

"But the profitability of big entities comes with responsibility. The decisions taken that help generate these profits, where these decisions may impact unfairly on everyday Australians, are matters central to this inquiry.
And here's more elements.
"The way the banks manage non-financial risk, especially as a result of action taken against them by financial watchdogs, is a relevant case in point here.
"We'll examine whether the benefits of a strong banking system are being shared fairly between customers, shareholders and employees.
"Besides inquiring about the future of bank branches, especially in our regions, we'll ask if major banks are doing enough for customers when things go wrong.

"That includes customers experiencing financial hardship, low-income Australians paying avoidable fees, scam and fraud victims, and people forced to take disputes to AFCA or the courts before obtaining an outcome, or startlingly, court action taken against mortgage holders without their knowledge, resulting in them having their homes taken off them.
"We'll look at workforce changes in the banks.
"Thousands of positions cut in Australia, only to be offshored.
"Those decisions warrant scrutiny, particularly where they involve technology, compliance and risk functions at a time when banks themselves tell us the risk environment is becoming more complicated.
"Just this morning we’re learning that one major bank (NAB) has been penalised for underpaying 65,000 of its workers millions of dollars over more than a decade.
"We'll look at the enormous technological transformation underway inside Australian banking."

ASIC sues Commonwealth Bank alleging tens of thousands of business customers overcharged fees

To another bank now, and the corporate regulator ASIC has announced it is suing the Commonwealth Bank for allegedly overcharging millions of dollars in fees to tens of thousands of business customers, many of them small businesses.
ASIC has started civil penalty proceedings against Australia's biggest bank, alleging customers were overcharged millions of dollars in fees they were never told about.

ASIC alleges CBA's CommBiz terms and conditions were misleading because they failed to clearly and accurately disclose all the fees business customers would be charged for direct debit and direct credit payments.
Business customers were told they would be charged a fee for a payment to or from a third-party account.
However, ASIC alleges CBA also charged an additional, undisclosed fee for the corresponding movement of money into or out of the customer's CommBiz account.
ASIC alleges that between November 2020 and May 31, 2025, about 42,000 CommBiz customers were overcharged about $8.5 million in fees.

Major bank NAB apologises and confirms remediation underway
Major bank NAB has responded to the Fair Work Ombudsman's announcement this morning, confirming it underpaid staff from October 1, 2012 until now.
The bank confirmed it had been running a program to identify and remediate all affected staff, with the payroll review and remediation still ongoing.

NAB group executive people & culture, Sarah White, says the bank is also investing in improving employee systems, processes and support, including a new human resources information system and payroll platform.

"We take our payroll obligations extremely seriously as a basic element in employing people. We sincerely apologise for these unintended errors," she says."We have and will continue to remediate anyone who has been impacted."
"We take our payroll obligations extremely seriously as a basic element in employing people. We sincerely apologise for these unintended errors," she says.
"We have and will continue to remediate anyone who has been impacted."
Under EU requirements with the Fair Work Ombudsman, NAB will undertake activities to ensure ongoing compliance, which include:
• Finalising NAB’s payroll review and remediation program
• Implementing a new payroll platform and time-recording process
• Implementing board reporting processes
• Engaging a third-party auditor to conduct at least two audits to assess compliance.
NAB says it will notify customers directly, if it hasn’t already, if they have been affected by any payroll errors.
Key Event
NAB penalised for underpaying its workers millions of dollars over more than a decade
Major bank NAB is paying millions of dollars to underpaid workers as part of entering into an Enforceable Undertaking (EU) with the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO).
NAB will pay $127 million, plus $34 million in interest and $8 million in superannuation, to 65,999 underpaid workers nationwide over more than a decade.
The bank will also make a $2 million contrition payment to the Commonwealth Consolidated Revenue Fund, and has committed to a range of measures to ensure it complies with future workplace laws.
The contrition payment is the largest ever included in an Enforceable Undertaking executed by the Fair Work Ombudsman.
NAB’s undertaking also includes terms that commit it to comprehensive planning and implementation of any future enterprise agreement, which the FWO says is the first time this has happened.
Payments to impacted individual workers range from less than $5 to more than $87,000, including superannuation and interest, with an average back-payment of about $1,934.
NAB self-reported the underpayments to the Fair Work Ombudsman in late 2019, after realising it had made significant errors in implementing its then enterprise agreement.
This prompted NAB to conduct a broad review of employee entitlements that identified non-compliance issues dating back to 2012.
Underlying causes of NAB’s underpayments included:
• Deficiencies in governance processes and compliance oversights
• Inadequate record-keeping
• Legacy payroll technology
• Limited investment in specialist capability relevant to payroll operations
The bank also failed to:
• Adequately capture time-and-attendance data for staff
• Accrue staff leave correctly
• Misapply and fail to apply various entitlements under successive enterprise agreements.

How to increase your home's climate resilience

Following on from the last post, AHURI researchers found that standards for new housing need strengthening and modernising, which could be achieved by mandating basic, established CRHG resilience measures for heat, bushfire, flood, and cyclone risks.
Adelaide University Senior Research Fellow Dr Michaela Lang says hazard zones based on projected climate exposures should be expanded and used in adaptation guidance.

"The risk is resilience standards will be based on scattered evidence and lag emerging climate realities," she says."Living systematic reviews, like those used in medical research, provide a blueprint for a continuously updated system to guide response based on new evidence and technologies."
"The risk is resilience standards will be based on scattered evidence and lag emerging climate realities," she says.
"Living systematic reviews, like those used in medical research, provide a blueprint for a continuously updated system to guide response based on new evidence and technologies."
Dr Lang says that's because the climate and level of risk are constantly changing.
The research found climate resilience could also be built into the Nationwide House Energy Rating Scheme, with better transparency to alert potential buyers and renters.
This could include updating the Existing Homes Disclosure Framework to require sellers and landlords to flag when a property falls below a minimum energy standard.
AHURI also says household energy security could improve through backup power supplies, including home batteries, and the installation of underground power lines in the regions.
The research also recommends that governments scale up retrofitting, prioritising basic and established CRHG measures.

The research says retrofitting could also be achieved by setting minimum resilience standards for rentals, targeted incentive programs to encourage upgrades to insulation, shading, air sealing and ventilation, and providing low-interest loans for structural retrofits.
Key Event
Improving Australian homes and households for climate extremes
New research from the independent national research institute dedicated to housing, AHURI, shows how to prepare Australia’s housing stock against future climate change events.
The study has developed guidelines that match climate change adaptation measures to current and future local climate conditions, rating each measure on:
• Its track record
• Level of innovation
• Whether it amplifies other risks
Adelaide University Senior Research Fellow Dr Michaela Lang, who has led the study, says the research addresses serious gaps in how Australia protects homes from climate change.

"Australia lacks a central source of guidance on climate resilience," she says."The National Construction Code and Nationwide House Energy Rating Scheme include some requirements but do not account for future climate conditions."
"Australia lacks a central source of guidance on climate resilience," she says.
"The National Construction Code and Nationwide House Energy Rating Scheme include some requirements but do not account for future climate conditions."
The proposed climate-ready housing guidelines (CRHG) from AHURI include measures for new and existing homes, matched to the risks they address, including bushfires, floods, cyclones and extreme heat.
This could include
• Adaptations like fire-rated shutters
• Innovative solutions like smart windows that switch between opaque and transparent or close in high winds
• Vacuum insulation panels
"Interviews with practitioners and householders show households can manage climate risks through more affordable temporary measures, as well as permanent home improvements," Dr Lang says.
Big Four bank bosses to be grilled over two days
It's time.
AI. Job cuts. High mortgage rates. Inflation. The economy.
It's all on the table for the bosses of Australia's largest banks who will be questioned by parliamentarians over two days, starting this morning.
The House of Representatives Standing Committee on Economics will hold its second set of annual public hearings with the CEOs of Australia’s big four banks in Canberra from 9.15AM AEDT.
Here's some words from the Committee Chair Ed Husic, a former Labor minister:
"Australia’s four major banks play an important role in the national economy. Decisions they make can impact many individuals, households and businesses.’
"It’s critical that the public are able to understand how the four major banks make the decisions they do, considering the impact these decisions have on the lives of everyday Australians.

"In recent weeks, the banks have revealed growth in their profits while also announcing they will cut jobs in Australia and outsource work offshore. The committee will focus on how these decisions serve the interests of its Australian customers and employees.’

"The committee particularly looks forward to hearing how the banks are serving their customers, how they are managing a range of risks, and how they are using artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies."
